
# Basics of Android Phones: Your Friendly Guide to Getting Started


---


## What Is This in Plain English?


Cast your mind back to the 1970s and the family television set. To change the channel, you had one dial. To adjust the volume, you had another. Every function had its own dedicated knob or button, and once you learned where each one was, the TV practically ran itself.


An Android phone works on exactly the same idea — except instead of physical dials, everything is a picture (called an **icon**) on a glass screen that responds to your fingertip. Each picture launches one thing: the phone icon starts a call, the camera icon takes a photo. Once you learn what each picture means, the phone becomes just as simple as that old television set.


The word "Android" simply refers to the operating system — think of it as the brand of engine inside the phone. Samsung, Google, Motorola, and many others all make Android phones, the same way Ford, Chevrolet, and Dodge all make cars that run on gasoline.


---


## Getting to Know the Physical Phone


Before touching the screen, let's learn the outside of the phone first — like reading the controls on the back of an appliance before plugging it in.


**The Screen:** The large, flat glass surface on the front. This is where everything happens. It responds to a light touch of one finger.


**The Power Button:** Usually found on the right-hand side of the phone, about halfway down. It is a small rectangular button, slightly raised so you can feel it. Press it once to wake the screen up. Press and hold it for two seconds to turn the phone fully off or on.


**The Volume Buttons:** Two buttons stacked on top of each other, usually on the left side of the phone. The top button makes sound louder. The bottom button makes it quieter. They often feel slightly ridged so your fingers can find them without looking.


**The Charging Port:** A small oval-shaped slot on the very bottom of the phone. This is where you plug in the charging cable each night — similar to plugging a lamp into a wall socket.


**The Front Camera:** A tiny circular lens at the top center of the screen. It is about the size of a match head. This is used for video calls so the other person can see your face.

> 💡 **Pro Tip:** If your screen goes dark and won't respond, don't panic. Simply press the **Power Button** once with your finger. The screen will light back up and ask you to swipe or enter your PIN, just like unlocking a front door.

---


## Part 1: Waking Up and Unlocking Your Phone


Think of your phone's lock screen like the locked glass door of a shop. You can see a little through the window, but you need a key to get inside.

1. Press the **Power Button** once on the side of your phone. The screen will light up and show the time, date, and possibly some notifications — small alert messages from your apps.
2. You will need to unlock the phone to get inside. Your phone will use one of these methods:

| Unlock Method        | What It Looks Like                                                            |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **PIN**              | A 4 or 6 digit number you type in, like an ATM code                           |
| **Pattern**          | You draw a shape by connecting dots on a grid                                 |
| **Fingerprint**      | Press your fingertip to a small oval sensor on the back or front of the phone |
| **Face Recognition** | Simply look at the screen and it unlocks automatically                        |

1. Once unlocked, the screen will open to your **Home Screen** — the main page of your phone, with all your app icons displayed like photos pinned to a corkboard.
> 🛡️ **Safety Alert:** Always use a PIN, fingerprint, or face lock on your phone. An unlocked phone is like a purse left open on a bus seat. If your phone is ever lost or stolen, a lock keeps your personal information safe from strangers.

---


## Part 2: Understanding Your Home Screen


The Home Screen is your starting point — the equivalent of the front hallway of your home, where you can see the doors to every room.


**App Icons:** These are the small square or circular pictures arranged in rows on your screen. Each one opens a different application — a program that does one specific job. Tap any icon once with your fingertip to open it.


**The Dock:** At the very bottom of the screen, you will usually see a row of 4 or 5 icons that stays the same no matter what. This is called the **Dock**, and your most important apps live here — typically the Phone, Messages, Internet browser, and Camera apps.


**The Notification Bar:** At the very top of the screen, you will see a thin strip showing small symbols. These are quiet alerts — a little envelope means you have a message, a Wi-Fi symbol (which looks like curved lines forming a fan shape, similar to radio waves) means you are connected to the internet.


**Swiping Between Pages:** If you have many apps, they may not all fit on one screen. Gently place your finger in the middle of the screen and slide it to the left — as if turning a page in a book. A second page of icons will appear. Slide right to go back.

> 💡 **Pro Tip:** If you ever get lost inside an app and can't find your way back to the Home Screen, look for a small button at the very bottom of the screen that looks like a **circle** or a **house shape**. Tapping that will always bring you safely home.

---


## Part 3: The Three Navigation Buttons


At the very bottom of an Android screen, you will find either three buttons or a single bar. These are your navigation controls — like the reverse, stop, and play buttons on an old VCR.


**The Back Button** — looks like a left-pointing arrow (◁). Tap this to go back one step, the same way you would back out of a room you walked into by mistake.


**The Home Button** — looks like a simple circle (○) or a small house shape (⌂). Tap this to return to your Home Screen from anywhere on the phone, no matter how deep inside an app you have wandered.


**The Recent Apps Button** — looks like a square (□) or three short horizontal lines stacked like a tiny ladder. Tap this to see all the apps you have opened recently, displayed like a deck of cards fanned out. You can swipe each one away to close it.

> 💡 **Pro Tip:** Some newer Android phones have replaced these three buttons with a single thin bar at the bottom of the screen. In that case, you simply swipe up from that bar to go Home, swipe up and hold to see recent apps, and swipe from the left or right edge to go Back. It takes a little practice, but feels quite natural within a day or two.

---


## Part 4: Making a Phone Call


Despite everything a smartphone can do, making a call is still wonderfully straightforward.

1. Find the **Phone** app on your Home Screen or in your Dock. It looks like an old-fashioned telephone handset — a curved shape you would have recognized immediately in 1975 — usually on a green background.
2. Tap it once to open it.
3. You will see a screen with three tabs along the top or bottom. Look for one that shows a grid of numbers — like a telephone keypad. Tap on it.
4. Tap the numbers of the person you want to call, just as you would dial a telephone.
5. Tap the **green button** (it looks like a telephone handset pointing downward) to start the call.
6. When you are finished, tap the **red button** (it looks like a handset pointing downward on a red background) to hang up.

**Calling Someone from Your Contacts:**

1. In the Phone app, look for a tab that shows a small silhouette of a person, or the word **Contacts**. Tap it.
2. Scroll through the alphabetical list until you find the person's name.
3. Tap their name once, then tap the green phone icon next to their number to call them.
> 🛡️ **Safety Alert:** If you receive a call from a number you do not recognize, it is perfectly fine not to answer. Let it go to voicemail. If it is important, the person will leave a message. Never call back an unknown number that texts you asking you to do so — this is a very common phone scam.

---


## Part 5: Sending and Reading Text Messages


A text message is like a short written note that travels instantly to another person's phone — a modern telegram, if you will.

1. Find the **Messages** app. It looks like a speech bubble — the same shape you see in comic strips when a character is talking — usually in green or blue.
2. Tap it to open it. You will see a list of your recent conversations.
3. To start a new message, look for a button in the bottom-right corner that looks like a **pencil and paper**, or a **plus sign (+)**. Tap it.
4. A box will appear at the top asking for a name or number. Type the name of someone in your Contacts, or type a phone number directly.
5. Tap the large white box near the bottom of the screen — this is where you type your message.
6. A keyboard will appear from the bottom of the screen, just like typewriter keys but displayed on the glass. Type your message by tapping the letters.
7. When finished, tap the button that looks like a **paper airplane** or an **arrow pointing to the right** to send your message.
> 💡 **Pro Tip:** If typing feels difficult, look for a small **microphone icon** on the keyboard — it usually sits near the spacebar. Tap it and simply speak your message out loud. The phone will type it for you automatically. Speak slowly and clearly, and say the word "period" or "comma" when you want punctuation.

---


## Part 6: Connecting to Wi-Fi


Wi-Fi is your home's invisible internet connection — like a radio signal that floats through your walls and connects your phone to the internet without any wires.

1. Open the **Settings** app. It looks like a gray gear wheel — a cog, like the ones inside an old mechanical clock.
2. Tap on **Wi-Fi** or **Network & Internet**, then tap **Wi-Fi**.
3. Make sure the toggle switch at the top is turned **on** — slid to the right and showing blue or green, like a light switch in the on position.
4. You will see a list of nearby Wi-Fi networks. Your home network will have the name you gave it when you set up your internet (for example, "Smith Family Wi-Fi" or "Netgear_247").
5. Tap on your network name.
6. A box will appear asking for your **password**. This is the Wi-Fi password — often found on a sticker on the back or bottom of your internet router (the small black or white box your internet provider installed, usually with blinking lights on the front).
7. Type in the password carefully — it is case-sensitive, meaning capital and lowercase letters matter — and tap **Connect**.
8. After a few seconds, you will see the word **Connected** appear beneath your network name. You are online.
> 🛡️ **Safety Alert:** When you are away from home — at a café, a doctor's office, or a shopping center — you may see public Wi-Fi networks available. Avoid doing anything sensitive on public Wi-Fi, such as checking your bank account or entering passwords. Public Wi-Fi is like having a conversation in a crowded room — others can sometimes listen in.

---


## Part 7: Adjusting the Text Size (Making Everything Bigger)


If the words on screen feel too small, you can make them larger very easily.

1. Open the **Settings** app — the gray gear wheel icon.
2. Scroll down and tap **Display**.
3. Look for **Font Size** or **Text Size** and tap on it.
4. You will see a slider — a horizontal bar with a small circle you can drag left or right, similar to the volume slider on an old stereo system. Drag the circle to the right to make text larger.
5. A preview at the top of the screen will show you exactly how the new size looks before you confirm. Adjust until it feels comfortable for your eyes.
> 💡 **Pro Tip:** You can also make all the icons and everything on screen larger — not just text. In **Display** settings, look for **Display Size** or **Screen Zoom** and slide that to the right as well. Many people find a slightly larger display size makes the whole phone easier to use.

---


## How to Stay Safe While Using Your Android Phone


**Lock your phone every time you set it down.** Press the Power Button once to put the screen to sleep. This keeps your information private from anyone who picks it up.


**Only download apps from the official Google Play Store.** The Play Store app looks like a colorful triangle — similar to a "play" button on a record player — on a white background. Never download apps from links sent to you in a text message or email, even if the message appears to come from someone you know.


**Update your phone when it asks you to.** When a small message appears saying "A software update is available," accept it. Updates fix security problems, the same way a locksmith improves a faulty lock. Tap **Install** and let the phone restart — it usually takes less than 10 minutes.


**Never share your PIN or password with anyone over the phone.** No company — not Google, not Samsung, not your phone carrier — will ever call you and ask for your PIN. Anyone who does is attempting a scam.


**When in doubt, don't tap.** If a message pops up that feels alarming — "Your phone has a virus! Tap here now!" — do not tap anything. Press the Home Button to return to your Home Screen and ask a trusted family member or friend to look at it with you.

> 🛡️ **Safety Alert:** If you ever feel pressured, confused, or rushed by something happening on your phone — stop. Set the phone down. No genuine emergency ever requires you to act on your phone within seconds. Real problems can wait five minutes while you call someone you trust.

## A Quick Reference Card


Cut this out or take a photo of it to keep handy.


| I Want To...          | What To Do                                  |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Wake up my phone      | Press the **Power Button** once             |
| Go back one step      | Tap the **Back Arrow** (◁)                  |
| Go to the Home Screen | Tap the **Circle** (○) or **House** button  |
| Make a call           | Tap the **green telephone handset** icon    |
| Send a text           | Tap the **speech bubble** icon              |
| Connect to Wi-Fi      | **Settings > Wi-Fi**                        |
| Make text bigger      | **Settings > Display > Font Size**          |
| Turn up the volume    | Press the **top Volume Button** on the side |


---


## You Are Doing Wonderfully


Learning a new device at any age takes patience and practice. Every person who now uses a smartphone fluently was once exactly where you are — looking at a screen full of unfamiliar pictures and wondering where to begin.


Start with just one section from this guide each day. By the end of a week, the phone will begin to feel familiar. By the end of a month, you may find yourself wondering how you ever managed without it.


If you would like hands-on help, your local library, senior center, or phone carrier store almost certainly offers free technology help sessions. You are never expected to learn this alone.
